title-group.article-title: Longitudinal patient-reported pain during radioligand therapy for metastatic prostate cancer.

contrib-group.aff: Great Lakes Cancer Consortium, Detroit, MI
Riverside University Medical Center, Chicago, IL

abstract.p: Background: Patient-reported pain interference is common among patients receiving radioligand therapy for metastatic prostate cancer, but its trajectory during and after treatment is not consistently captured in routine oncology practice. We characterized longitudinal symptom burden and factors associated with clinically meaningful worsening. Methods: Participants completed the Brief Pain Inventory at baseline, after cycle 2, end of treatment, and 3 months after treatment. Mixed-effects models evaluated change over time, and multivariable regression assessed baseline clinical and patient-reported predictors. A prespecified threshold was used to define clinically meaningful worsening from baseline. Results: The cohort included 156 patients. Mean symptom score was 4.8 at baseline, reached 3.6 at the period of greatest burden, and was 3.9 at the final assessment. Clinically meaningful worsening occurred in 39% of participants. In adjusted analysis, baseline skeletal disease burden was independently associated with worse longitudinal symptom scores (β=0.26, p=0.002). Completion rates exceeded 80% at each scheduled assessment. Conclusions: Pain interference changed substantially over the treatment course among patients receiving radioligand therapy for metastatic prostate cancer. Routine longitudinal assessment may identify patients who would benefit from earlier supportive care, particularly those with baseline skeletal disease burden. Research Sponsor: None.
